belief: Jesus died for other people’s sins, but not ones as bad as mine.
meta: A Christian look at the false belief that Jesus died for other people’s sins but not ones as bad as yours, with Scripture, questions, and homework for replacing it with the truth.
origins: Deep shame about something in your past. Being told by a parent or church that certain sins put you beyond help. Comparing your worst moments with other people’s best. Having confessed many times without feeling forgiven. A sensitive conscience, or intrusive thoughts that seem to prove you are especially bad.
teaches: Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul, who once persecuted Christians, called himself the worst of them. Christ’s blood cleanses from all sin. God promises to make scarlet sins white as snow and to remove them as far as the east is from the west. Where sin is great, grace is greater. Your sin is not bigger than the cross.
self_statements: What I did is too terrible to forgive.
Grace is for other people, not me.
If people knew, they’d agree I’m beyond saving.
I’ve sinned too many times for God to keep forgiving.
God forgives small sins, but mine are different.
I don’t deserve to be forgiven.
errors: Making your sin look bigger than Christ’s sacrifice.
Believing that God’s promises apply to everyone except you.
Concluding “I still feel guilty, so I must not be forgiven.”
Calling yourself “unforgivable” instead of “a sinner Jesus came to save.”
Dismissing every verse about forgiveness as not meant for you.
questions: Does 1 John 1:7 say Jesus cleanses from some sin, or from all sin?
Is my sin bigger than the cross of Christ?
Paul called himself the worst of sinners. Did God refuse to forgive him?
Am I making my feelings a higher authority than God’s Word?
If I were God, would I want my forgiveness to have a limit?
Is refusing forgiveness a kind of pride, as if my sin is too special for grace?
Who first told me I was beyond forgiveness?
truth: Jesus died for all my sins, including the ones I am most ashamed of. His blood cleanses me from all sin. My worst moments are not stronger than His grace. When I confess, He forgives, and He removes my sins as far as the east is from the west. I am forgiven because of what He did, not because I feel worthy.
hw_questions: Does Jesus cleanse from some sin, or all sin?
Is my sin bigger than the cross?
If God forgave Paul, why not me?
Am I trusting my feelings over God’s Word?
Is my sin really too special for grace?
Who first told me I was beyond forgiveness?
hw_truths: Jesus’ blood cleanses me from all sin.
My sin is not bigger than the cross.
Christ came to save sinners like me.
Where my sin increased, grace increased all the more.
God has removed my sins as far as the east is from the west.
I am forgiven because of Jesus, not because of my feelings.
log: Each time the old shame returns, write: “That debt was nailed to the cross,” and the date.
name_example: ‘Come now, let us reason together,’ says the LORD. ‘Though Sarah’s sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they will become like wool.’
actions: Write the sin you are most ashamed of on a slip of paper,
read Colossians 2:13–14 over it, then tear it up and throw it away.
pray 1 John 1:9, then thank God instead of confessing the same sin again.
Read the story of the sinful woman in Luke 7:36–50,
and notice how Jesus treats her.
Talk with a pastor or trusted Christian friend
about what forgiveness means, and write down what you learn.
prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You that You came to save sinners, and that Your blood cleanses me from all sin. Help me reject the lie that my sins are too great for You. When shame returns, remind me that my debt was nailed to the cross. Teach me to receive Your forgiveness and to live in the freedom You paid for. In Your name, Amen.
songs: God’s forgiveness addresses lingering guilt and fear of condemnation.
God’s cleansing grace challenges the belief that shame or sin makes a person beyond restoration.
Christ’s sacrifice answers guilt and the effort to pay for one’s own sins.
This classic hymn locates salvation and sustaining hope in grace rather than merit.
